claim: Low-protein (LP) diets extend the lifespan of diverse species.
source: Low-protein (LP) diets extend the lifespan of diverse species and are associated with improved metabolic health in both rodents and humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established finding in the field.

claim: Low-protein diets are associated with improved metabolic health in both rodents and humans.
source: Low-protein (LP) diets extend the lifespan of diverse species and are associated with improved metabolic health in both rodents and humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established finding.

claim: HP-fed mice gain significantly more fat mass than LP-fed mice when not exercising.
source: We find that despite having lower food consumption than the LP group, HP-fed mice gain significantly more fat mass than LP-fed mice when not exercising, while weight pulling protected HP-fed mice from this excess fat accretion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Weight pulling protected HP-fed mice from excess fat accretion.
source: We find that despite having lower food consumption than the LP group, HP-fed mice gain significantly more fat mass than LP-fed mice when not exercising, while weight pulling protected HP-fed mice from this excess fat accretion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: HP-fed mice have lower food consumption than LP-fed mice.
source: We find that despite having lower food consumption than the LP group, HP-fed mice gain significantly more fat mass than LP-fed mice when not exercising, while weight pulling protected HP-fed mice from this excess fat accretion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The HP diet augmented exercise-induced hypertrophy of the forearm flexor complex.
source: The HP diet augmented exercise-induced hypertrophy of the forearm flexor complex, and weight pulling ability increased more rapidly in the exercised HP-fed mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and H.

claim: Weight pulling ability increased more rapidly in the exercised HP-fed mice.
source: The HP diet augmented exercise-induced hypertrophy of the forearm flexor complex, and weight pulling ability increased more rapidly in the exercised HP-fed mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: Exercise did not protect from HP-induced changes in glycemic control.
source: Surprisingly, exercise did not protect from HP-induced changes in glycemic control.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3A-E.

claim: HP diets can augment muscle hypertrophy induced by resistance exercise without negative effects on fat mass.
source: Our results confirm that HP diets can augment muscle hypertrophy and accelerate strength gain induced by resistance exercise without negative effects on fat mass, and also demonstrate that LP diets may be advantageous in the sedentary.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: LP diets may be advantageous in the sedentary.
source: Our results confirm that HP diets can augment muscle hypertrophy and accelerate strength gain induced by resistance exercise without negative effects on fat mass, and also demonstrate that LP diets may be advantageous in the sedentary.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings showing better metabolic outcomes in sedentary LP-fed mice.

claim: Low-protein diets are associated with reduced rates of diabetes in human longitudinal studies.
source: Dietary protein in particular has been shown to have a critical role in the regulation of metabolic health and longevity; low-protein (LP) diets are associated with reduced rates of diabetes and other age-related diseases in human longitudinal studies, and promote leanness and insulin sensitivity in human randomized clinical trials of metabolically unhealthy adults (Ferraz-Bannitz et al., 2022; Fontana et al., 2016; Levine et al., 2014; Sluijs et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Low-protein diets promote leanness and insulin sensitivity in human randomized clinical trials of metabolically unhealthy adults.
source: Dietary protein in particular has been shown to have a critical role in the regulation of metabolic health and longevity; low-protein (LP) diets are associated with reduced rates of diabetes and other age-related diseases in human longitudinal studies, and promote leanness and insulin sensitivity in human randomized clinical trials of metabolically unhealthy adults (Ferraz-Bannitz et al., 2022; Fontana et al., 2016; Levine et al., 2014; Sluijs et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In mice, LP, high carbohydrate diets reduce adiposity.
source: In mice, LP, high carbohydrate diets reduce adiposity, improve glucose tolerance, and extend lifespan (Hill et al., 2022; Richardson et al., 2021; Solon-Biet et al., 2014; Solon-Biet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In mice, LP, high carbohydrate diets improve glucose tolerance.
source: In mice, LP, high carbohydrate diets reduce adiposity, improve glucose tolerance, and extend lifespan (Hill et al., 2022; Richardson et al., 2021; Solon-Biet et al., 2014; Solon-Biet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In mice, LP, high carbohydrate diets extend lifespan.
source: In mice, LP, high carbohydrate diets reduce adiposity, improve glucose tolerance, and extend lifespan (Hill et al., 2022; Richardson et al., 2021; Solon-Biet et al., 2014; Solon-Biet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Some short-term studies have found that HP intake improves glucose control in adults with type 2 diabetes.
source: In addition to promoting satiety, some short-term studies have found that HP intake improves glucose control in adults with type 2 diabetes (Dong et al., 2013; Gannon et al., 2003; Seino et al., 1983), and HP diets are recommended for physically active individuals to support muscle growth and strength improvements (Andersen et al., 2005; Willoughby et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: HP diets are recommended for physically active individuals to support muscle growth and strength improvements.
source: In addition to promoting satiety, some short-term studies have found that HP intake improves glucose control in adults with type 2 diabetes (Dong et al., 2013; Gannon et al., 2003; Seino et al., 1983), and HP diets are recommended for physically active individuals to support muscle growth and strength improvements (Andersen et al., 2005; Willoughby et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Both exercise and amino acids activate the mechanistic target of TOR (mTOR) protein kinase.
source: Both exercise and amino acids activate the mechanistic target of TOR (mTOR) protein kinase, which stimulates the protein synthesis machinery needed to stimulate skeletal muscle hypertrophy (Schiaffino et al., 2021; Simcox and Lamming, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: mTOR stimulates the protein synthesis machinery needed to stimulate skeletal muscle hypertrophy.
source: Both exercise and amino acids activate the mechanistic target of TOR (mTOR) protein kinase, which stimulates the protein synthesis machinery needed to stimulate skeletal muscle hypertrophy (Schiaffino et al., 2021; Simcox and Lamming, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics recommends consuming 1.2–2.0 g of protein per kg of body weight per day in physically active individuals.
source: To support this process, the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics recommends consuming 1.2–2.0 g of protein per kg of body weight (BW) per day in physically active individuals (Thomas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published recommendation.

claim: The Recommended Daily Allowance for sedentary people is 0.8 g/kg BW of protein.
source: These protein estimations are substantially higher than the Recommended Daily Allowance for sedentary people of 0.8 g/kg BW, an amount intended to provide sufficient nutrients in 97.5% of people, but it remains controversial if protein intake above this level is detrimental in this population.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about dietary recommendations.

claim: Exercise reduces the risk of developing type 2 diabetes.
source: However, there is no data available to support such a surprising conclusion, and indeed the opposite is true: exercise reduces the risk of developing type 2 diabetes (Grøntved et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Seven-week-old C57BL/6J mice were randomized to groups of equal weight and body composition.
source: Seven-week-old C57BL/6J mice were randomized to groups of equal weight and body composition, and placed on either an LP (7% of calories from protein) or HP (36% of calories from protein) diet.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and methods used in the study.

claim: The LP diet contained 7% of calories from protein.
source: Seven-week-old C57BL/6J mice were randomized to groups of equal weight and body composition, and placed on either an LP (7% of calories from protein) or HP (36% of calories from protein) diet.
evidence: This describes the diet composition used in the study.

claim: The HP diet contained 36% of calories from protein.
source: Seven-week-old C57BL/6J mice were randomized to groups of equal weight and body composition, and placed on either an LP (7% of calories from protein) or HP (36% of calories from protein) diet.
evidence: This describes the diet composition used in the study.

claim: The two diets were isocaloric with calories from fat kept at 19%.
source: The two diets were isocaloric as calories from fat were kept at 19%, and carbohydrates were reduced in the HP diet to compensate for the increased calories from amino acids.
evidence: This describes the diet composition used in the study.

claim: Carbohydrates were reduced in the HP diet to compensate for the increased calories from amino acids.
source: The two diets were isocaloric as calories from fat were kept at 19%, and carbohydrates were reduced in the HP diet to compensate for the increased calories from amino acids.
evidence: This describes the diet composition used in the study.

claim: On both a per-animal and a weight-normalized basis, LP diet-fed mice ate more than HP-fed mice.
source: On both a per-animal and a weight-normalized basis, LP diet-fed mice ate more than HP-fed mice, consistent with the satiating effect of dietary protein (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: There was no effect of WP on food consumption.
source: There was no effect of WP on food consumption (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: HP-fed mice gained more weight over the course of 18 weeks despite consuming fewer calories than LP-fed mice.
source: Despite consuming fewer calories than LP-fed mice – the two diets have the same caloric density – HP-fed mice gained more weight over the course of 18 wk.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: By the end of the experiment, HP-fed WP mice had gained significantly less weight than HP-fed sham-exercised controls.
source: By the end of the experiment, HP-fed WP mice had gained significantly less weight than HP-fed sham-exercised controls (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: HP-fed mice gained significantly more lean mass than LP-fed mice.
source: As we expected based on previous studies investigating the effects of an LP diet as well as data demonstrating the beneficial effects of protein on muscle growth (Andersen et al., 2005; Willoughby et al., 2007), HP-fed mice gained significantly more lean mass than LP-fed mice, although surprisingly exercise did not affect this gain (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1E and citations to previous studies.

claim: Exercise did not affect lean mass gain.
source: As we expected based on previous studies investigating the effects of an LP diet as well as data demonstrating the beneficial effects of protein on muscle growth (Andersen et al., 2005; Willoughby et al., 2007), HP-fed mice gained significantly more lean mass than LP-fed mice, although surprisingly exercise did not affect this gain (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Sham-exercised HP-fed mice gained substantially more body fat than their LP-fed counterparts.
source: In accordance with our previous results, we found that sham-exercised HP-fed mice gained substantially more body fat than their LP-fed counterparts; however, we found that WP was protective against these effects (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: WP was protective against HP-induced body fat gain.
source: In accordance with our previous results, we found that sham-exercised HP-fed mice gained substantially more body fat than their LP-fed counterparts; however, we found that WP was protective against these effects (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) was significantly heavier in sham-exercised HP-fed mice than in WP HP-fed mice.
source: We found that the inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) and epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) were significantly heavier in sham-exercised HP-fed mice than in WP HP-fed mice (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) was significantly heavier in sham-exercised HP-fed mice than in WP HP-fed mice.
source: We found that the inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) and epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) were significantly heavier in sham-exercised HP-fed mice than in WP HP-fed mice (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There was a statistically significant effect of diet on liver weight, with HP-fed mice having heavier livers.
source: Finally, there was a statistically significant effect of diet on liver weight, with HP-fed mice having heavier livers, an effect that was larger in sham-exercised mice than in WP mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The effect of HP diet on liver weight was larger in sham-exercised mice than in WP mice.
source: Finally, there was a statistically significant effect of diet on liver weight, with HP-fed mice having heavier livers, an effect that was larger in sham-exercised mice than in WP mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: HP-fed groups did not have increased hepatic lipid accumulation despite increased liver weight.
source: Despite the increased liver weight of the HP groups, they did not have increased lipid accumulation; instead, there was a nonsignificant trend toward both larger and a greater number of liver lipid droplets in the LP-fed groups, with no effect of WP (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: There was no difference in average iWAT adipocyte size or number.
source: There was no difference in average iWAT adipocyte size or number (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: LP-fed mice had improved glucose tolerance relative to HP-fed mice.
source: We performed glucose and insulin tolerance tests; in agreement with our previous findings, we found that LP-fed mice had improved glucose tolerance relative to HP-fed mice, and there was a trend (p=0.0788) toward a positive effect of WP on glucose tolerance (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a trend (p=0.0788) toward a positive effect of WP on glucose tolerance.
source: We performed glucose and insulin tolerance tests; in agreement with our previous findings, we found that LP-fed mice had improved glucose tolerance relative to HP-fed mice, and there was a trend (p=0.0788) toward a positive effect of WP on glucose tolerance (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LP-fed mice were more insulin-sensitive than HP-fed mice under sham conditions.
source: Similarly, while LP-fed mice were more insulin-sensitive than HP-fed mice under sham conditions, we did not observe a difference between LP and HP-fed mice that performed WP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was no difference in insulin sensitivity between LP and HP-fed mice that performed WP.
source: Similarly, while LP-fed mice were more insulin-sensitive than HP-fed mice under sham conditions, we did not observe a difference between LP and HP-fed mice that performed WP (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HP-fed mice had higher fasting blood glucose than LP-fed mice under sham exercise conditions.
source: In agreement with a model in which high dietary protein is deleterious to sedentary animals, we observed that HP-fed mice had higher fasting blood glucose than LP-fed mice under sham exercise conditions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: WP did not correct the difference in fasting blood glucose between HP and LP-fed mice.
source: Interestingly, WP did not correct this difference – instead, we saw that there was an overall effect of HP-feeding toward increased fasting blood glucose level in both sham-exercised and WP mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HP-fed WP mice had significantly higher insulin levels than LP-fed WP mice.
source: A similar effect of diet was noted on fasting insulin levels, with HP-fed WP mice having significantly higher insulin levels than LP-fed WP mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: LP WP mice had significantly better insulin sensitivity than HP-fed WP mice as calculated via the HOMA2-IR method.
source: In agreement with the overall effect of diet on fasting glucose and insulin levels, we also observed an overall effect of diet on insulin sensitivity calculated via the HOMA2-IR method, with LP WP mice having significantly better insulin sensitivity than HP-fed WP mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: LP-fed sham mice had significantly higher levels of FGF21 in their blood compared to their HP-fed counterparts.
source: We and others have previously shown that an LP diet increases fasting FGF21 levels in C57BL/6J male mice (Green et al., 2022; Hill et al., 2022), and we determined that LP-fed sham mice had significantly higher levels of FGF21 in their blood compared to their HP-fed counterparts (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3F and citations to previous studies.

claim: WP mice had a strong overall trend (p=0.0751) toward lower FGF21 levels.
source: Interestingly, WP mice had a strong overall trend (p=0.0751) toward lower FGF21 levels, and LP-fed WP mice did not have significantly higher FGF21 levels than HP-fed WP mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: LP-fed mice had higher ketone levels than HP-fed mice.
source: FGF21 promotes ketogenesis, and in agreement with our FGF21 data we observed an overall effect of diet on fasting blood ketone levels, with LP-fed mice having higher ketone levels than HP-fed mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: There was a significant interaction of diet and exercise on ketone levels, with WP lowering ketone levels in HP-fed mice.
source: Intriguingly, there was a significant interaction of diet and exercise, with WP lowering ketone levels in HP-fed mice.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: There was an overall increase of triglycerides in WP-fed mice, which was statistically significant in HP-fed mice.
source: Surprisingly, while diet had no effect on triglyceride or lipid levels, there was an overall increase of triglycerides in WP-fed mice, which was statistically significant in HP-fed mice (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: There was no effect of diet or exercise on blood levels of cholesterol.
source: There was no effect of diet or exercise on blood levels of cholesterol (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: HP-fed mice tended to consume less food than LP-fed mice, although this did not reach statistical significance.
source: In agreement with our prior home-cage observations and the well-known satiating effect of dietary protein, we observed that HP-fed mice tended to consume less food than LP-fed mice, although this did not reach statistical significance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was no overall effect of exercise on spontaneous activity.
source: There was no overall effect of exercise on spontaneous activity, but in the light phase there was an overall effect of diet, with LP-fed mice moving more (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the light phase there was an overall effect of diet on spontaneous activity, with LP-fed mice moving more.
source: There was no overall effect of exercise on spontaneous activity, but in the light phase there was an overall effect of diet, with LP-fed mice moving more (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was an overall effect of diet on RER, with mice consuming the LP diet having a higher RER during the dark cycle.
source: As we anticipated, there was an overall effect of diet on RER, with mice consuming the LP diet having a higher RER during the dark cycle, reaching statistical significance in the WP groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: There was a significant effect of the LP diet on energy expenditure, both on a per-animal basis and when weight was considered as a covariate.
source: In agreement with previous studies, we observed a significant effect of the LP diet on energy expenditure, both on a per-animal basis and when weight was considered as a covariate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Resistance exercise did not have an overall effect on either RER or energy expenditure.
source: Resistance exercise did not have an overall effect on either RER or energy expenditure.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: There was a significant overall effect of diet on the maximum load mice were able to pull during their training sessions.
source: In agreement with this, we observed an significant overall effect of diet on the maximum load mice were able to pull during their training sessions as well as the corresponding area under the curve (AUC) (Figure 4A), consistent with HP-fed mice being able to pull more weight.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The difference in maximum weight pulled was statistically significant only during the third week of the training regimen.
source: However, the difference was smaller than we had anticipated and was statistically significant only during the third week of the training regimen; the maximum weight pulled by LP-fed and HP-fed mice appeared to converge after approximately 10 wk of training (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The maximum weight pulled by LP-fed and HP-fed mice appeared to converge after approximately 10 weeks of training.
source: However, the difference was smaller than we had anticipated and was statistically significant only during the third week of the training regimen; the maximum weight pulled by LP-fed and HP-fed mice appeared to converge after approximately 10 wk of training (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was no overall effect of diet on the average number of sets per training bout.
source: There was no overall effect of diet on the average number of sets per training bout (Figure 4B) or the average number of stimulatory touches by the investigator (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was no overall effect of diet on the average number of stimulatory touches by the investigator.
source: There was no overall effect of diet on the average number of sets per training bout (Figure 4B) or the average number of stimulatory touches by the investigator (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was an overall positive effect of an LP diet on inverted cling time.
source: We observed an overall positive effect of an LP diet on inverted cling time, an effect that persisted (p=0.0597) in sham-exercised mice when we analyzed inverted cling performance with weight as a covariate (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There was no overall effect of either diet or training on raw rotarod performance.
source: Although we observed no overall effect of either diet or training on raw rotarod performance (Figure 4F), we observed a significant positive effect of an HP diet on the rotarod performance of sham-exercised mice when weight was considered as a covariate (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There was a significant positive effect of an HP diet on the rotarod performance of sham-exercised mice when weight was considered as a covariate.
source: Although we observed no overall effect of either diet or training on raw rotarod performance (Figure 4F), we observed a significant positive effect of an HP diet on the rotarod performance of sham-exercised mice when weight was considered as a covariate (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: There was an overall positive effect of both an HP diet and WP on FDL mass.
source: We have previously shown that WP induces hypertrophy in the flexor digitorum longus (FDL) (Zhu et al., 2021), and as we expected we found an overall positive effect of both an HP diet and WP on FDL mass, both in absolute terms and when normalized to either body mass or tibia length (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 5A-C and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The greatest muscle mass was observed in mice that completed the WP regimen while consuming an HP diet.
source: We observed the greatest muscle mass in mice that completed the WP regimen while consuming an HP diet, but HP diet consumption alone also had a positive effect on absolute FDL mass and FDL mass normalized to tibia length (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: HP diet consumption alone had a positive effect on absolute FDL mass and FDL mass normalized to tibia length.
source: We observed the greatest muscle mass in mice that completed the WP regimen while consuming an HP diet, but HP diet consumption alone also had a positive effect on absolute FDL mass and FDL mass normalized to tibia length (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: There was no change to leak respiration in the FDL.
source: Using complex I-linked substrates pyruvate, glutamate, and malate, we found no change to leak respiration (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Complex I-driven respiration at 0.25 mM, 0.5 mM, and 5.5 mM ADP was not different in any intervention group.
source: We next evaluated sub-saturating and saturating complex I-driven respiration by providing ADP at 0.25 mM, 0.5 mM, and 5.5 mM; none of these parameters were different in any intervention group (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: There was no difference in any group following succinate addition for complex I + II-linked respiration.
source: Furthermore, we saw no difference in any group following succinate addition for complex I + II-linked respiration (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: There was no positive effect of either resistance exercise or HP diet on quadricep mass.
source: Overall, there was no positive effect of either resistance exercise or HP diet on quadricep mass (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and E), while the mass of the soleus and plantaris muscles were positively impacted by dietary protein but largely resistant to the benefits of WP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C and F–G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and E.

claim: The mass of the soleus and plantaris muscles were positively impacted by dietary protein but largely resistant to the benefits of WP.
source: Overall, there was no positive effect of either resistance exercise or HP diet on quadricep mass (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and E), while the mass of the soleus and plantaris muscles were positively impacted by dietary protein but largely resistant to the benefits of WP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C and F–G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C and F-G.

claim: There were strong effects of WP and a significant interaction between dietary protein and exercise on the mass of the forearm flexor complex.
source: However, there were strong effects of WP and a significant interaction between dietary protein and exercise on the mass of the forearm flexor complex, with the HP-fed WP mice having the greatest forearm flexor complex mass in raw weight and when normalized to tibia length (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and H.

claim: HP-fed WP mice had the greatest forearm flexor complex mass in raw weight and when normalized to tibia length.
source: However, there were strong effects of WP and a significant interaction between dietary protein and exercise on the mass of the forearm flexor complex, with the HP-fed WP mice having the greatest forearm flexor complex mass in raw weight and when normalized to tibia length (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and H.

claim: There were clear overall effects of both dietary protein and WP on bicep and forearm diameter.
source: Finally, we assessed the maximum diameter of the bicep and forearm (Figure 6A) and found that there were clear overall effects of both dietary protein and WP on bicep and forearm diameter (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Bicep diameter was maximized under HP WP conditions.
source: Bicep diameter was maximized under HP WP conditions (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: HP-fed WP mice had the largest forearm diameter of all groups.
source: There was a less potent but still significant effect on the forearm; HP-fed WP mice had the largest forearm diameter of all groups (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Nonexercising LP-fed mice had the smallest bicep and forearm diameter.
source: Conversely, nonexercising LP-fed mice had the smallest bicep and forearm diameter (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: There was no significant difference in mid-belly cross-sectional area (CSA) or the number of fibers per cross section in the FDL.
source: There was no significant difference in mid-belly cross-sectional area (CSA) or the number of fibers per cross section (Figure 7B and C), indicating that alterations in dietary protein or WP might not induce hyperplasia of muscle fibers (Jorgenson and Hornberger, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Alterations in dietary protein or WP might not induce hyperplasia of muscle fibers.
source: There was no significant difference in mid-belly cross-sectional area (CSA) or the number of fibers per cross section (Figure 7B and C), indicating that alterations in dietary protein or WP might not induce hyperplasia of muscle fibers (Jorgenson and Hornberger, 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in fiber number and supported by a citation.

claim: There was an overall effect of diet on the CSA of muscle fibers, with individual fibers in HP-fed mice having greater CSA.
source: There was, however, an overall effect of diet on the CSA of muscle fibers, with individual fibers in HP-fed mice having greater CSA (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There was an overall effect of diet on the size of type IIA, type IIB, and type IIX fibers, with HP diets increasing fiber size.
source: When we analyzed fiber-type-specific CSA, we observed an overall effect of diet on the size of type IIA, type IIB, and type IIX fibers, with HP diets increasing fiber size (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 7F-H.

claim: There was an effect of resistance exercise on the size of type IIA and type IIX fibers, with WP inducing fiber hypertrophy.
source: We also saw an effect of resistance exercise on the size of type IIA and type IIX fibers, with WP inducing fiber hypertrophy (Figure 7F and H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 7F and H.

claim: There was a significant interaction between dietary protein and WP on the size of type I fibers, with the greatest hypertrophy occurring in HP-fed WP mice.
source: Finally, we observed a significant interaction between dietary protein and WP on the size of type I fibers, with the greatest hypertrophy occurring in HP-fed WP mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In sedentary humans increased consumption of dietary protein is associated with cancer, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes, as well as increased mortality.
source: Paradoxically, in sedentary humans increased consumption of dietary protein is associated with cancer, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes, as well as increased mortality (Lagiou et al., 2007; Levine et al., 2014; Mittendorfer et al., 2020; Sluijs et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: LP diets and diets with reduced levels of specific essential amino acids promote healthspan and lifespan in flies and rodents.
source: In agreement with the potential for dietary protein to negatively impact health, LP diets and diets with reduced levels of specific essential amino acids promote healthspan and lifespan in flies and rodents (Flores et al., 2023; Green et al., 2023; Juricic et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2014; Lees et al., 2014; Orentreich et al., 1993; Richardson et al., 2021; Solon-Biet et al., 2014; Yap et al., 2020), and short-term protein restriction improves the metabolic health of metabolically unhealthy adult humans (Ferraz-Bannitz et al., 2022; Fontana et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Short-term protein restriction improves the metabolic health of metabolically unhealthy adult humans.
source: In agreement with the potential for dietary protein to negatively impact health, LP diets and diets with reduced levels of specific essential amino acids promote healthspan and lifespan in flies and rodents (Flores et al., 2023; Green et al., 2023; Juricic et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2014; Lees et al., 2014; Orentreich et al., 1993; Richardson et al., 2021; Solon-Biet et al., 2014; Yap et al., 2020), and short-term protein restriction improves the metabolic health of metabolically unhealthy adult humans (Ferraz-Bannitz et al., 2022; Fontana et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Studies in healthy, resistance-trained individuals show HP diets can be consumed without negative effects on body composition.
source: However, our results are consistent with studies in healthy, resistance-trained individuals that show HP diets can be consumed without negative effects on body composition (Antonio et al., 2015; Antonio et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Both HP and resistance training are necessary for inducing hypertrophy of slow-twitch, oxidative fiber types (type I fibers) in the FDL.
source: Finally, when broken down to individual muscle fiber types, we saw an increase in type 1 muscle fiber size in the FDL of the HP + WP group, which indicates that both HP and resistance training are necessary for inducing hypertrophy of slow-twitch, oxidative fiber types.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only the HP + WP group showed increased type I fiber size.

claim: The findings of specific fiber-type hypertrophy in the FDL in response to WP are consistent with previous observations.
source: These findings are consistent with specific fiber-type hypertrophy previously observed in the FDL in response to WP (Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: HP feeding resulted in larger type IIA fibers than LP in the context of both sham training and WP.
source: We saw a similar induction of growth by both diet and training in type IIA fibers, which are fast-twitch, oxidative, and glycolytic. Here, HP feeding resulted in larger fibers than LP in the context of both sham training and WP, which is consistent with human recommendations that increased dietary protein supports muscle hypertrophy (Thomas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 7F and a citation to human recommendations.

claim: There was no difference in hypertrophy of type IIX and IIA fibers in the FDL induced by WP when fed an LP or HP diet.
source: A striking takeaway observed here is that there was no difference in hypertrophy of type IIX and IIA fibers in the FDL induced by WP when fed an LP or HP diet.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 7F and H.

claim: Both resistance training and HP diets individually and in combination optimize growth of muscle fibers.
source: Though these changes occurred in just one muscle, and effects on other muscles may vary, our results indicate that both resistance training and HP diets individually and in combination optimize growth of muscle fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fiber-type analysis data.

claim: The negative effects of an HP diet on body composition are eliminated in mice performing progressive resistance exercise training.
source: Specifically increasing protein consumption has – as we anticipated based on both animal and human data – negative effects on the metabolic health of mice that are not exercising. However, the negative effects of an HP diet on body composition are eliminated in mice performing progressive resistance exercise training.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The ultimate max load the HP and LP-fed mice could pull by the end of 12 weeks was indistinguishable despite clear differences in muscle mass.
source: While mice consuming an HP diet gained strength during WP more quickly than LP-fed mice, the ultimate max load the HP and LP-fed mice could pull by the end of 12 wk was indistinguishable despite clear differences in muscle mass.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sedentary individuals would be metabolically healthier if consuming an LP diet.
source: We hypothesize that further studies will find that sedentary individuals would be metabolically healthier if consuming an LP diet.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion based on the study findings.

claim: A precision nutrition approach to metabolic health must consider not only diet, sex, and genetic variation, but also take into account activity level.
source: Finally, our results suggest that a precision nutrition approach to metabolic health must consider not only diet, sex, and genetic variation, but also take into account activity level.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study findings.

claim: Weight pulling does not result in weight loss.
source: Importantly, unlike aerobic exercise models like treadmill running, WP does not result in weight loss, allowing us to study the metabolic impact of exercise without confounding changes in body weight.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the weight pulling model used in the study.

claim: In humans, mitochondrial respiration is increased after both aerobic and resistance training regimens.
source: In humans, mitochondrial respiration is increased after both aerobic and resistance training regimens (Konopka et al., 2015; Konopka et al., 2019; McKenna et al., 2022; Robinson et al., 2017), perhaps due to the high energetic demands imposed by protein synthesis (Rolfe and Brown, 1997; Waterlow, 1984), which is upregulated following resistance training (Ogasawara et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Protein synthesis is upregulated following resistance training.
source: In humans, mitochondrial respiration is increased after both aerobic and resistance training regimens (Konopka et al., 2015; Konopka et al., 2019; McKenna et al., 2022; Robinson et al., 2017), perhaps due to the high energetic demands imposed by protein synthesis (Rolfe and Brown, 1997; Waterlow, 1984), which is upregulated following resistance training (Ogasawara et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The mitochondrial response to varying amounts of dietary protein with or without resistance training has not been examined.
source: However, the mitochondrial response to varying amounts of dietary protein with or without resistance training has not been examined, and we therefore performed high-resolution respirometry in permeabilized muscle fibers from the FDL.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: Sex, genetic background, and age impact the metabolic response to dietary protein.
source: We examined only young inbred C57BL/6J male mice, and we have previously shown that sex, genetic background, and age impact the metabolic response to dietary protein (Green et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The hormone FGF21 is responsive to exercise in mice and humans.
source: The hormone FGF21, which is induced by an LP diet, is responsive to exercise in mice and humans (Haghighi et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022), but we did not observe increased FGF21 in the LP weight-trained group, suggesting another mechanism could be at play.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: FGF21 promotes ketogenesis.
source: FGF21 promotes ketogenesis, and in agreement with our FGF21 data we observed an overall effect of diet on fasting blood ketone levels, with LP-fed mice having higher ketone levels than HP-fed mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about FGF21 function.

claim: An RER of close to 1.0 indicates that carbohydrates are being preferentially utilized for energy production.
source: We examined respiratory exchange ratio (RER) by calculating the ratio of O2 consumed and CO2 produced; an RER of close to 1.0 indicates that carbohydrates are being preferentially utilized for energy production, while a value near 0.7 indicates that lipids are the predominant energy source (Bruss et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about RER interpretation and supported by citations.

claim: An RER value near 0.7 indicates that lipids are the predominant energy source.
source: We examined respiratory exchange ratio (RER) by calculating the ratio of O2 consumed and CO2 produced; an RER of close to 1.0 indicates that carbohydrates are being preferentially utilized for energy production, while a value near 0.7 indicates that lipids are the predominant energy source (Bruss et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about RER interpretation and supported by citations.

claim: Rotarod and inverted cling outcomes can be improved by voluntary aerobic exercise (wheel running).
source: As rotarod and inverted cling outcomes can be improved by voluntary aerobic exercise (wheel running) (Graber et al., 2015), this could be the result of either the type of exercise or the precise muscles strengthened by WP vs. aerobic exercise.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.
